Research protocol: TCGA nested-CV stablr-DIABLO comparison

1 Scope and status of this protocol

Non-executable research protocol. This page specifies the benchmark and cache-reading contract. No TCGA head-to-head result is bundled or counted as release evidence. The external dataset, long-running fits, exact candidate, and output cache must be pinned before execution.

The compact TCGA vignette shows the workflow. This vignette defines the evidence-generating benchmark and reports results only when an external cache is available. It compares stablr and mixOmics DIABLO on the same three-class PAM50 breast cancer task: Basal, Her2, and LumA.

The design is nested cross-validation. Outer folds estimate generalisation. Inner folds tune the models. Feature selection is repeated inside each training split, rather than performed once on the full dataset before validation. That distinction is the difference between a benchmark and an optimistic story.

The head-to-head uses mRNA and miRNA only. The protein block in mixOmics::breast.TCGA is available only for the original training samples, while all 220 samples have mRNA and miRNA. Excluding protein keeps both methods on the same samples and blocks.

The heavy computation is not run while rendering this vignette. It is executed outside the package through SLURM and cached as an RDS file. Until that cache is present, the vignette is a methodological protocol rather than bundled empirical evidence.

2 Methodological audit

This workflow was checked against the nestedcv vignette guidance for p >> n biomedical prediction. No filter or feature-selection result is computed on the full dataset before cross-validation. STABL selection, downstream multinomial refitting, DIABLO component tuning, and DIABLO keepX tuning all occur inside the relevant training split before a held-out outer fold is predicted.

The design also follows p >> n variable-selection practice:

  • predictors are passed as numeric matrices and model scaling is left inside the fitting procedures rather than learned globally before CV;
  • the outer loop estimates performance, while the inner loop selects candidates and tuning parameters;
  • stablr uses knockoff artificial features for FDP-aware stability selection;
  • the deliverable is a recurrence profile over outer folds, not a single definitive biomarker list;
  • no naive post-selection p-values are reported.

The benchmark is still exploratory. Confirmatory extensions would include external cohort validation and refitting unpenalised subtype models on only the most recurrent features, with explicit post-selection qualification.

3 Running the benchmark on SLURM

The cache setup is configured as follows.

use_external_cache <- identical(
  tolower(Sys.getenv("STABLR_USE_EXTERNAL_TCGA_CACHE", unset = "false")),
  "true"
)
experiments_root <- Sys.getenv(
  "STABLR_EXPERIMENTS_ROOT",
  unset = file.path(dirname(getwd()), "stablr-experiments")
)
analysis_dir <- file.path(experiments_root, "analysis")
analysis_script <- file.path(analysis_dir, "run_tcga_nestedcv.R")
tcga_cache_complete <- function(path) FALSE
if (use_external_cache && file.exists(analysis_script)) {
  source(analysis_script)
} else if (use_external_cache) {
  tcga_cache_complete <- function(path) file.exists(path)
}

cache_path <- if (use_external_cache) {
  file.path(analysis_dir, "cache", "tcga_nestedcv_results.rds")
} else {
  "<external TCGA cache disabled>"
}
slurm_cmd <- if (use_external_cache) {
  paste("sbatch", file.path(analysis_dir, "tcga_nestedcv.slurm"))
} else {
  "Set STABLR_USE_EXTERNAL_TCGA_CACHE=true before using external artifacts."
}
has_results <- FALSE  # updated by cache-status chunk below
cat("Expected cache:", cache_path, "\n")
#> Expected cache: <external TCGA cache disabled>
cat("Submit command:", slurm_cmd, "\n")
#> Submit command: Set STABLR_USE_EXTERNAL_TCGA_CACHE=true before using external artifacts.

The output reports the expected cache path and the SLURM submit command. When the external cache is not enabled, both entries are replaced by the corresponding placeholder messages.

The cache status is then checked.

has_results <- tcga_cache_complete(cache_path)
if (!has_results) {
  cat(
    "Nested-CV cache is not available yet.\n",
    "No TCGA head-to-head benchmark results are bundled in this render.\n",
    "Opt in to external artifacts, submit the SLURM job above, then render this notebook again.\n",
    sep = ""
  )
}
#> Nested-CV cache is not available yet.
#> No TCGA head-to-head benchmark results are bundled in this render.
#> Opt in to external artifacts, submit the SLURM job above, then render this notebook again.

When the cache is absent, the chunk prints a notice that no TCGA head-to-head benchmark results are bundled in the render and that the SLURM job must be submitted before the notebook is rendered again.

4 Analysis design

The cache records the exact settings used by the SLURM runner.

The settings are printed when the cache is available.

res <- readRDS(cache_path)
str(res$settings)

The output shows the pinned settings of the cached run.

stablr uses multinomial stability selection with knockoff artificial features. The candidate workflows are mRNA-only, miRNA-only, and early fusion across mRNA and miRNA. Candidate choice is based on inner-CV balanced error rate.

DIABLO uses the mixOmics multiblock sPLS-DA workflow: block.plsda() and perf() choose the number of components, tune.block.splsda() tunes keepX, and the locked outer-fold model is evaluated with weighted-vote centroids.dist predictions.

5 Predictive performance

When the cache is present, the performance table is the first readout. The confusion matrices show where the methods make their mistakes, which is often more informative than a single accuracy number. Without the cache, this section intentionally produces no numeric claim.

The overall performance table is printed as follows.

res$performance

The table reports the outer-fold performance of both methods.

The confusion matrices are printed for both methods.

stabl_conf <- table(
  Truth = res$stablr$outer_predictions$truth,
  Predicted = res$stablr$outer_predictions$predicted
)
diablo_conf <- table(
  Truth = res$diablo$outer_predictions$truth,
  Predicted = res$diablo$outer_predictions$predicted
)

cat("stablr confusion matrix:\n")
print(stabl_conf)
cat("\nDIABLO confusion matrix:\n")
print(diablo_conf)

Each matrix cross-tabulates truth and prediction over the pooled outer-fold predictions. The off-diagonal counts identify the classes that each method confuses.

Per-fold metrics are computed and paired across methods as follows.

fold_metric <- function(pred) {
  by_fold <- split(pred, pred$fold_id)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(by_fold), function(id) {
    m <- tcga_metrics(by_fold[[id]]$truth, by_fold[[id]]$predicted)
    data.frame(fold_id = id, m, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))
}

stabl_fold <- fold_metric(res$stablr$outer_predictions)
diablo_fold <- fold_metric(res$diablo$outer_predictions)
paired <- merge(stabl_fold, diablo_fold, by = "fold_id",
                suffixes = c("_stablr", "_DIABLO"))
paired$delta_BER <- paired$balanced_error_rate_stablr -
  paired$balanced_error_rate_DIABLO
paired$delta_accuracy <- paired$accuracy_stablr - paired$accuracy_DIABLO
summary(paired[, c("delta_BER", "delta_accuracy")])

The output summarises the paired per-fold differences in balanced error rate and accuracy between the two methods.

6 Feature comparison

Feature recurrence is the biomarker-side counterpart to predictive performance. A recurrent feature is not merely selected once; it survives across many outer training splits.

The overlap table is printed as follows.

res$feature_comparison$overlap

The table summarises the agreement between the feature sets of the two methods.

The most recurrent features per block are listed as follows.

recurrence <- res$feature_comparison$recurrence
head(recurrence[order(recurrence$block, -recurrence$recurrence), ], 30)

The output shows the 30 most recurrent feature-block combinations, ordered by block and by decreasing recurrence.

The features selected by both methods are extracted as follows.

shared <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(recurrence, recurrence$block), function(tab) {
  stabl_feats <- tab$feature[tab$method == "stablr"]
  diablo_feats <- tab$feature[tab$method == "DIABLO"]
  tab[tab$feature %in% intersect(stabl_feats, diablo_feats), ]
}))
shared[order(shared$block, shared$feature, shared$method), ]

The output lists the features that appear in both the stablr and the DIABLO selections, ordered by block, feature, and method.

7 Exported artifacts

The SLURM runner writes these files next to the cache.

The exported files are listed when the cache is available.

list.files(dirname(cache_path), pattern = "tcga_nestedcv", full.names = TRUE)

The listing contains the cache file and the CSV exports whose names match tcga_nestedcv. The CSV files are intended for manuscript tables and supplement material: performance, feature recurrence, and feature overlap by omic block.

8 Interpreting stablr vs DIABLO results

Predictive and feature-level outputs should be read together. A method that wins on balanced error rate (BER) is not automatically preferable for biomarker discovery, and vice versa.

8.1 Predictive layer

Observation Interpretation
Lower outer-fold BER for DIABLO Latent multiblock structure may explain class separation better than sparse per-feature STABL + refit on this cohort.
Lower outer-fold BER for stablr Inner-CV candidate choice (mRNA / miRNA / early fusion) plus multinomial refit may capture signal DIABLO’s fixed component budget misses.
Similar BER, different confusion patterns Methods trade errors across classes; inspect per-class recall before declaring a winner.
Large fold-to-fold BER variance Dataset is small (220 samples); treat point estimates as exploratory.

Negative delta_BER (stablr − DIABLO) favours DIABLO; positive favours stablr. Paired fold deltas should be reported with bootstrap confidence intervals (see inst/analysis/BENCHMARK_PLAN.md, Phase 2).

8.2 Feature and biomarker layer

Observation Interpretation
High recurrence, modest overlap with DIABLO Stability selection and component sparsity surface partially complementary feature sets.
stablr features recurrent, absent from DIABLO loadings May reflect block-specific marginal signal stabilised by resampling, not captured in shared latent factors.
DIABLO selectVar features absent from stablr support May load strongly on components without surviving FDP+ thresholding across bootstraps.
stablr selects more features per fold FDP threshold and lambda grid control sparsity; DIABLO sparsity is governed by keepX.

8.3 When each method is the better tool

Criterion Prefer stablr Prefer DIABLO
Primary deliverable Named biomarker list with stability evidence Integrative classification + component visualisation
False-discovery diagnostic Knockoff / FDP+ estimate built in Not part of the default workflow
Outcome types gaussian, binomial, multinomial, Cox Classification-centric multiblock sPLS-DA
Block coupling Cooperative rho or fusion modes Design matrix + shared latent space
Ecosystem glmnet, native R, Python STABL parity mixOmics tutorials, circos, network plots
Compute profile Many bootstraps × lambda grid Component + keepX tuning (typically faster per fold)

For Python STABL parity (selection semantics, not prediction contests), see docs/PYTHON_TO_R_MAPPING.md.
